top_choice_rationale: Adonis (P001) is my first choice on the common criteria. The poetry reworks the idiom of Arabic verse through myth, fragmentation and a sustained argument with inherited forms, as in Songs of Mihyar the Damascene and A Time Between Ashes and Roses. That is a distinctive voice and a language-level formal achievement, and the oeuvre is long and fully formed enough to be judged as a whole, which is the standard I apply to a whole authorship rather than a single work. The citation should credit the poetry, with the poetics named only as what informs the verse. The essays cannot carry the case if the poems cannot. My evidence has real limits. Prosody, diction and allusion reach me only through translations and secondary accounts, and I cannot verify corpus coverage or show that the later decades, including the long poem-book Al-Kitab, deepen the project rather than repeat it. I rank Cărtărescu (P002) second. His large prose architecture is distinctive and assessable now, and I could support him as the final recommendation if confidence in the Arabic poems cannot be reached. Carson (P003) is a serious candidate whose breadth beyond a few well-known works I cannot yet judge, and her hybrid and book-object forms travel poorly. I place her above no award. Translation limits apply to every shortlisted writer and argue for careful reading and openly stated reliance, not for withholding the prize, so P000 is last.
recusal_note: none apparent from profile. The documented connections are collegial: service with Olsson, Mattson, Sem-Sandberg and Palm, and election in the same renewal round as Mattson. The profile records no personal, professional or translation tie to Adonis, Cărtărescu, Carson or any other shortlisted writer. My own literary practice is context, not evidence of preference.
